name: Awngi
confidence_why: Hetzron (1969, 1976, 1997) describes a penultimate demarcative stress operating alongside tone, Worku Gela (1986) instead puts stress on the first syllable (final in adjectives, adverbs and imperatives), and Joswig (2010), the fullest phonology of the language, treats Awngi as a two-level tone language and could not confirm any independent stress, so first-hand descriptions disagree on whether Awngi has word stress at all and, if it does, where it falls. The Kunfäl (Kulazngi) dialect is described separately below from its own source, with a three-level tone inventory.

new_statements.quote: By all definitions above, Kulazngi is a tone language, or it is not a mere pitch-accent language, because every syllable in a word bears low, mid, or high tone having a lexical as well as a grammatical function. A significant number of lexical items of the same word class show meaning variation due to pitch variation only. Pitch also plays a role to express grammatical distinction. [p.44] ... In this study, Kulazngi has three level (high, low, mid) and one contour (HL) tones. Each level tone can appear with monosyllabic and disyllabic words. While high and low tones have no positional restriction, mid tone never occurs word initially in polysyllabic words; it does not occur sequentially (as M.M) either. [p.45]

Pitch also plays a role to express grammatical distinction." p.73 (printed p.45, sec. 2.3.2 Toneme Inventory) has the second half verbatim: "In this study, Kulazngi has three level (high, low, mid) and one contour (HL) tones. Each level tone can appear with monosyllab…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kunfäl/Kulazngi is described as a lexical and grammatical tone language (H, M, L, HL) in which every syllable carries a tone; the grammar gives no rule for word stress and never says where stress falls. The earlier sketch by Zelealem Leyew (n.d., pp.12-13) says it cannot yet be determined whether Kulisi is a pitch accent or a tone language and whether its pitch distinctions are 'distinct from stress or pitch accent'; Yaregal 2016 resolves this in favour of tone.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Tonal distribution restrictions only: mid tone not word-initial in polysyllables and never in M.M sequences; HL contour restricted to mono- and disyllabic nouns; minimal pairs e.g. múrí (H.H) 'snake' vs mùrí (L.H) 'village'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (nouns, adjectives, verbs in citation form); data from the Bagʷsa dialect of Kulazngi in Jawi wereda. No statement on phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: kunf1238 'Kunfal' is a Glottolog Bookkeeping code: ISO 639-3 xuf was retired on 2008-01-14 (change request 2007-044) and merged into awn Awngi after the 2005 SIL survey found the K'wara/Alefa/Jawi lowland Agaw to be a dialect of Awngi (72-74 % lexical similarity, one-sided intelligibility). The speakers reject 'Kunfäl' (pejorative Amharic exonym); they call themselves Kulisi Agaw (Zelealem Leyew) or Kulaz / Kulazngi (Yaregal 2016), and the older shifted-from language is Kumpalngi. The deciding source (Yaregal 2016) describes the Bagʷsa dialect of Kulazngi in Jawi wereda, Awi Zone. The parent language Awngi (awng1244) is already in the catalog coded 'conflict' (Hetzron penult stress vs Joswig 2010 'no evidence' vs Worku 1986 initial/final); the Kulazngi statement is tone-only and belongs under awng1244 as a dialect record unless the catalog counts Kunfäl as a separate entity — by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) a retired code does not make a separate language, so the catalog gate should decide whether this is a new row or an addition to awng1244.

tone_statements.quote: All this leads to the conclusion that the low tone of Hetzron and Palmer really is just a phonetic variation of the mid tone, reserved for the vowel /a/ on open utterance-final syllables. Therefore it is reasonable to claim that there are only two phonemic tone levels in Awngi, high and low. ... The conflicting evidence from Hetzron and Worku certainly makes it questionable whether there is any stress of intensity in Awngi at all. sources.note: Argues Palmer's and Hetzron's four tones (H, M, L, falling) reduce to two phonemic levels H and L (their low = phonetic variant of mid on utterance-final open /a/); falling = H+L on one word-final syllable, derived by floating-tone rules (Rule 1 floating tone assignment, Rule 2 H-floating + final L -> fall), no rising tones; weighs a pitch accent analysis and rejects it because most affixes carry their own tones and floating tones occur; stress of intensity (Hetzron penult vs Worku initial/final) 'not observed in the data collected for this study'.

sources.note: Secondhand via Yaregal 2016 sec. 2.3.2 (held text read): 'Kulazngi has two level tones, high and low (Zelealem's forthcoming: 13)', with four contrastive pairs (e.g. 'village' vs 'snake'), some presumed former tonal pairs now homophonous in his Jawi data, and the question pitch accent vs tone left open for further investigation; i.e. two levels H/L, not H/M/L; report itself not opened (academia.edu login; Koeln URL dead, no archived copy at the Internet Archive).
